# Lens 2B.1 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler choose diplomacy, compromise, and de-escalation when credible peaceful alternatives existed, rather than treating force as the preferred first option?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **mixed but weighted toward force as the preferred instrument**. Xi executed two real diplomatic de-escalations (the March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement and the November 2023 Biden–Xi summit's mil-to-mil reset) and made some rhetorical compromise (NFU reaffirmation), but on every concrete 2023 dispute where peaceful alternatives existed — Taiwan, South China Sea, India LAC, Iran nuclear program, Syria CW compliance, JCPOA revival, cross-strait dialogue, India border deconfliction — Xi either pursued military/grey-zone coercion, suspended diplomatic engagement, or declined a peaceful-alternative path that was on offer.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — diplomacy/compromise/de-escalation positives

### 1. Brokering of the Iran–Saudi rapprochement (10 March 2023)

- **Claim A1.** In March 2023, after multi-month Beijing-mediated talks, Xi brokered a diplomatic normalization between Iran and Saudi Arabia, ending a seven-year rupture. This is the most consequential single 2023 diplomatic de-escalation by Xi.
  - **Source:** "Iran–Saudi Arabia relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_relations ("However, in March 2023, after discussions brokered by China, Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to reestablish relations").
  - **Source:** "What the Iran-Saudi Agreement Reveals About China's Approach to Conflict Management," Guy Burton, *The Diplomat*, 15 March 2023 — https://thediplomat.com/2023/03/what-the-iran-saudi-agreement-reveals-about-chinas-approach-to-conflict-management/.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (positive — diplomatic de-escalation), 1B.4, 1B.10, 8G.4, 8G.8.

### 2. November 2023 Biden–Xi summit and mil-to-mil reset

- **Claim A2.** The 15 November 2023 Woodside/San Francisco summit was Xi's first in-person meeting with Biden in over a year. The summit agreed to **resume US-China military-to-military communications** (suspended since the August 2022 Pelosi visit), established a bilateral AI dialogue, and produced cooperation on fentanyl precursor chemicals. This is a real diplomatic de-escalation act.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("15 November – U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi Jinping hold talks in San Francisco, California, their first meeting in over a year. The talks are described as being positive with 'real progress' being made on key issues such as drug trafficking and artificial intelligence").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (positive — diplomatic act, channel preservation), 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.8, 8G.3.

### 3. NFU reaffirmation at the Biden–Xi summit

- **Claim A3.** Xi reaffirmed China's unconditional no-first-use nuclear posture at the 15 November 2023 summit — a rhetorical compromise that signals continued Chinese restraint on nuclear first-use.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("In 1964, China adopted a policy of no-first-use (NFU) and called for an international NFU treaty, both of which it continues to advocate").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (rhetorical positive — restraint), 1B.2, 1B.10.

### 4. No personal Xi nuclear threat in 2023

- **Claim A4.** Across 2023, Xi did not personally issue nuclear threats, did not use apocalyptic or first-strike language, and did not link nuclear capability to coercion against Taiwan or any other state. This is a restraint-positive at the personal-rhetoric level.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (rhetorical positive), 1B.2.

### 5. Retained bilateral crisis-management architecture with India

- **Claim A5.** Throughout 2023, China maintained the bilateral India border architecture (Special Representatives mechanism, Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs, 1996 no-firearms agreement, brigade-level flag meetings). This is a diplomatic channel that Xi did not abrogate.
  - **Source:** "China–India relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93India_relations ("Border deconfliction mechanisms emerged, beginning with the 2003 Special Representatives … 1996 agreement forbids firearms and explosives near the LAC").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (positive — channel preserved), 1B.8.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — peaceful alternatives declined; force / coercion chosen

### 6. Taiwan: no diplomatic engagement, continued grey-zone coercion throughout 2023

- **Claim B1.** The Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis (initiated August 2022) continued throughout 2023 with PLA exercises, ADIZ incursions, naval patrols, and Coast Guard boardings. Xi did **not** engage with the KMT-CCP dialogue track, did **not** propose a cross-strait crisis-management framework, did **not** resume Cross-Strait Economic and Cultural Exchange, and did **not** accept any of the peaceful alternatives on offer. The diplomatic track remained frozen; the operational coercion track continued.
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis ("PLA exercises, maritime patrols and even Coast Guard boardings around the Taiwan Strait becoming routine in what has been defined as 'grey-zone tactics'" — 2023 pattern is a continuation).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternatives declined), 8G.6.

### 7. South China Sea: coercion campaign continued; no binding COC

- **Claim B2.** China's grey-zone coercion against the Philippines continued through 2023 (10 November 2023 "control measures" at Second Thomas Shoal). China did **not** conclude a binding ASEAN Code of Conduct, did **not** adjust the nine-dash-line claim, and did **not** accept any of the peaceful alternatives on offer. The 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling remained rejected.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 entry).
  - **Source:** "South China Sea disputes" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes (no 2023 binding COC adoption recorded).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternatives declined), 1B.8, 8G.5.

### 8. Iran nuclear program: 25-year cooperation deepened without WMD conditionality

- **Claim B3.** In February 2023, Iranian President Raisi made the first Iranian state visit to China in over 20 years; China continued to implement its 2021 25-year strategic cooperation agreement with Iran. Xi did **not** condition any of this cooperation on Iranian nuclear-program restraint, did **not** condition the March 2023 Iran–Saudi deal on JCPOA compliance, and did **not** lead a JCPOA revival push in 2023. China remained a JCPOA signatory in principle but did not exercise the leverage the 25-year agreement gives it.
  - **Source:** "China–Iran relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Iran_relations ("In February 2023, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi visited China in the first such visit by an Iranian leader to China in more than twenty years").
  - **Source:** "Iran–Saudi Arabia relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_relations ("However, in March 2023, after discussions brokered by China, Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to reestablish relations").
  - **Source:** "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action (no 2023 Chinese revival push).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternative declined), 1B.4, 1B.6.

### 9. Syria: 22 September 2023 partnership without CW conditionality

- **Claim B4.** On 22 September 2023, Syria's Assad (a regime with documented CW-use record) visited China and signed a Belt and Road strategic-partnership agreement. Xi did **not** condition the partnership on CW compliance, accountability for past use, or cooperation with OPCW processes.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("22 September – Syrian President Bashar al-Assad visits China, meets with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and signs a strategic partnership with China on infrastructure as part of China's Belt and Road Initiative").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful conditionality declined), 1B.6.

### 10. DPRK: limited sanctions enforcement despite peaceful alternatives

- **Claim B5.** Throughout 2023, China — as a permanent UNSC member and key DPRK trade partner — continued limited enforcement of UN Security Council sanctions on the DPRK. The DPRK continued its nuclear-program advancement and ballistic-missile testing (Hwasong-18 solid-fuel ICBM in April 2023, additional tests). Xi did **not** push for new UNSC sanctions and did **not** visibly tighten bilateral enforcement. Peaceful alternatives (sanctions tightening, US-China coordinated pressure) were on the table and declined.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("North Korea … are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles").
  - **Source:** "Sanctions against North Korea" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_North_Korea.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternative declined), 1B.6.

### 11. India LAC: military infrastructure continued, no 2023 disengagement

- **Claim B6.** Although Xi maintained the bilateral India border architecture (Claim A5), the underlying LAC standoff persisted through 2023 with no 2023 disengagement completed. Military infrastructure near the LAC continued to grow on the Chinese side, and no peaceful breakthrough was achieved.
  - **Source:** "China–India relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93India_relations ("military infrastructure near the LAC continues to grow").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (mixed — channel held but no progress), 8G.7.

### 12. Nuclear arms control: no 2023 engagement with New START, JCPOA, CTBT

- **Claim B7.** In 2023, China did **not** ratify the CTBT, did **not** offer to join or engage with New START, did **not** push for JCPOA revival, and did **not** publish any stockpile transparency figure. The 2023 backdrop was the worst year for global arms control in decades; China did not seize the opening to lead. Peaceful alternatives (treaty ratification, dialogue, transparency) were on the table.
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("9 Annex 2 states still need to take further action for the treaty to enter into force. 6 are signatories who have not ratified: China").
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START ("On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START").
  - **Source:** "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (strongly negative — peaceful alternatives declined), 1B.4, 1B.10.

### 13. Russia: no 2023 restraint despite peaceful alternatives

- **Claim B8.** Russia in 2023 suspended New START (21 February), withdrew CTBT ratification (November), stationed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus, and made repeated nuclear-coercion threats to NATO. Xi hosted Putin at the 3rd Belt and Road Forum (17–18 October 2023) and provided a high-profile platform for Putin's first meeting with an EU leader (Orbán) since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Xi did **not** use Chinese leverage to restrain Russian nuclear-coercion rhetoric or to push Russia back to the arms-control framework. Peaceful alternatives (Xi restraint on a nuclear-encouraging partner) were declined.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("17 October – Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold talks at the Belt and Road Initiative forum in Beijing").
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START.
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternative declined), 1B.6, 1B.4, 8G.7.

### 14. Domestic-repression alternative path declined in 2023

- **Claim B9.** Throughout 2023, Xi did **not** respond to peaceful expressions of grievance with restraint or compromise. The counter-responses were the Counterespionage Law (April–July 2023), the Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023), the Patriotic Education Law (October 2023), the August 2023 Xinjiang "success" declaration after the damning UN report, and the Rahile Dawut life sentence. The peaceful alternatives (release of political prisoners, opening of inquiry into Xinjiang, repeal of the HK NSL) were on the table and declined.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china (Xinjiang "success" declaration; Rahile Dawut life sentence; revised Counterespionage Law; Religious Activity Venues measures; Patriotic Education Law).
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternatives declined on repression), 8D, 8F.1.

### 15. Surveillance-tech export continued; no 2023 restraint

- **Claim B10.** Throughout 2023, Chinese firms (Huawei, Hikvision, Dahua, ByteDance / TikTok) continued to export AI-driven surveillance technology to authoritarian-leaning regimes. Xi did **not** join the April 2023 multilateral export-control framework, did **not** impose new export-restraint rules, and did **not** pause the bilateral pipelines that were on offer. Peaceful alternatives (multilateral restraint) were declined.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.1 (negative — peaceful alternative declined), 1B.9, 1B.10, 8F.1.

---

## C. Net reading for lens 2B.1

The 2023 evidence is **mixed — two real diplomatic de-escalations against many declined peaceful alternatives**:

- **Positive diplomatic acts:** Iran–Saudi rapprochement (March 2023); Biden–Xi summit and mil-to-mil reset (November 2023); NFU rhetoric; personal Xi rhetorical restraint; bilateral India channel preservation.
- **Declined peaceful alternatives:** Taiwan dialogue, South China Sea COC, Iran JCPOA conditionality, Syria CW conditionality, DPRK sanctions enforcement, Russia restraint, global arms control (CTBT ratification, New START engagement), India LAC disengagement, domestic-repression opening, surveillance-tech export restraint.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have used the November 2023 Biden summit and the March 2023 Iran–Saudi deal as templates for binding peaceful frameworks on Taiwan (cross-strait), Iran (JCPOA revival), and Russia (arms-control pressure), and would have imposed at least symbolic conditionality on the Syria deal. Xi did none of these.

The use of force — grey-zone coercion against the Philippines in the South China Sea, the operational Taiwan Strait pressure campaign, the continued PLA silo and arsenal buildup — was the **default 2023 instrument** for the territorial disputes Xi chose to prioritize. Diplomacy was the instrument Xi chose to deploy selectively, on issues where the cost of force was high (a Biden summit, an Iran–Saudi deal) and where the visible diplomatic achievement could be celebrated as a foreign-policy win.

**Net judgment: 2B.1 reads as mixed-to-negative for 2023 — Xi executed two notable diplomatic de-escalations but otherwise chose force / coercion / non-engagement as the preferred instrument for the majority of concrete 2023 disputes where credible peaceful alternatives existed. The pattern is consistent with a ruler for whom diplomacy is a tactical tool, not the default.**

---
